```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

The inner search of a nested run can use a fixed grid, a race, Bayesian
optimization or simulated annealing. Each search has a nested function
that takes the same design and workflow and returns the same kind of
result. A race spends fewer fits when some candidates (settings tried) are
clearly worse. The Bayesian and annealing searches propose candidates from
ranges rather than a fixed grid.

`vignette("nested-cv")` uses the grid. This page runs the other searches on
the same example. It then scores two more things on the same folds: a
workflow with nothing to tune, and a set of workflows.

```{r deps, include = FALSE}
needed <- c("tidymodels", "ranger")
missing_pkgs <- needed[
  !vapply(needed, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]
has_deps <- length(missing_pkgs) == 0L
```

```{r deps-notice, eval = !has_deps, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat(
  "This page attaches the **tidymodels** packages and fits random forests",
  "with the **ranger** package.",
  if (length(missing_pkgs) == 1L) {
    sprintf("The **%s** package is not installed here,", missing_pkgs)
  } else {
    sprintf(
      "The **%s** packages are not installed here,",
      paste(missing_pkgs, collapse = "** and **")
    )
  },
  "so the rest of this page has been skipped. Install",
  if (length(missing_pkgs) == 1L) "it" else "them",
  "and rebuild to see it.\n"
)

knitr::knit_exit()
```

```{r libraries, message = FALSE}
library(tidymodels)
library(nestedtune)
```

```{r deps-optional, include = FALSE}
has_finetune <- requireNamespace("finetune", quietly = TRUE)
has_race <- has_finetune &&
  all(vapply(
    c("lme4", "BradleyTerry2"),
    requireNamespace,
    logical(1),
    quietly = TRUE
  ))
```

## The setup

We reuse the design, the random forest and the grid from
`vignette("nested-cv")`.

```{r design}
set.seed(1)

folds <- nested_resamples(
  mtcars,
  outside = vfold_cv(v = 5),
  inside = vfold_cv(v = 5)
)

rf <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("regression")

wf <- workflow(mpg ~ ., rf)

grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(2L, 5L, 8L), min_n = c(2L, 10L))
```

The Bayesian and annealing searches propose their own candidates from
a range for each parameter. `tune_bayes()` does not
accept a range that depends on the data, such as that of `mtry`, so we set
it by hand. We also keep `min_n` within the grid's range, because its
default range is larger than an inner analysis set here.

```{r param-info}
params <- update(
  extract_parameter_set_dials(wf),
  mtry = mtry(c(2L, 8L)),
  min_n = min_n(c(2L, 10L))
)
```

## Bayesian optimization

`nested_tune_bayes()` runs `tune::tune_bayes()` in each outer fold. The
search scores `initial` starting candidates, then proposes `iter` more,
one at a time, from a Gaussian process model of the scores so far. We keep both small so
the page builds quickly.

```{r bayes}
set.seed(2)

bayes <- nested_tune_bayes(
  wf,
  folds,
  param_info = params,
  initial = 4,
  iter = 3
)

bayes
```

Each fold proposes candidates from its own scores, so the folds do not
search the same set, and the print says so.

## Racing

The racing functions take a grid. They score every candidate on a few
inner resamples first, and then stop scoring the candidates that are
clearly worse than the best. `nested_tune_race_anova()` decides with an
ANOVA model, and `nested_tune_race_win_loss()` decides with a model of
pairwise wins.

```{r race-notice, eval = !has_race, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
absent <- c("finetune", "lme4", "BradleyTerry2")
absent <- absent[!vapply(
  absent,
  requireNamespace,
  logical(1),
  quietly = TRUE
)]

cat(
  "The racing runs need the **finetune**, **lme4** and **BradleyTerry2**",
  "packages, and",
  if (length(absent) == 1L) "one of them is" else "some of them are",
  "not installed here:",
  paste0(paste0("**", absent, "**", collapse = ", "), "."),
  "The racing section",
  if (has_finetune) "has" else "and the simulated annealing section have",
  "been skipped. Install what is missing and rebuild to see them.\n"
)
```

```{r race-anova, eval = has_race}
set.seed(3)

race <- nested_tune_race_anova(wf, folds, grid = grid)

race
```

The inner metrics show how many resamples scored each candidate. Summed
over one metric, they give the fits each fold spent on tuning. A full grid
search costs `r nrow(folds$inner_resamples[[1]]) * nrow(grid)` fits per
fold.

```{r race-anova-inner, eval = has_race}
collect_inner_metrics(race) |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(fits = sum(n))
```

On this small example the race dropped few candidates. The win/loss race
is called the same way. Here are its fits per fold.

```{r race-win-loss, eval = has_race}
set.seed(4)

win_loss <- nested_tune_race_win_loss(wf, folds, grid = grid)

collect_inner_metrics(win_loss) |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(fits = sum(n))
```

## Simulated annealing

`nested_tune_sim_anneal()` runs `finetune::tune_sim_anneal()` in each
outer fold. Each proposal is a small random move from the current
candidate. It is kept when it scores better, and sometimes when it scores
worse. The control below turns off finetune's log of every move.

```{r anneal, eval = has_finetune}
set.seed(5)

anneal <- nested_tune_sim_anneal(
  wf,
  folds,
  param_info = params,
  initial = 3,
  iter = 3,
  control = finetune::control_sim_anneal(verbose_iter = FALSE)
)

anneal
```

## A workflow with nothing to tune

A tuned model is often compared with the same model at fixed settings,
here one of the grid's.
`nested_fit_resamples()` scores such a workflow on the same nested design.
Each outer fold fits the workflow on its analysis rows and scores it on its
assessment rows.

```{r baseline}
fixed_rf <- rand_forest(mtry = 2L, min_n = 10L, trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("regression")

set.seed(2)
baseline <- nested_fit_resamples(workflow(mpg ~ ., fixed_rf), folds)

collect_metrics(baseline)
```

Both runs used the same folds, so we can join their scores fold by fold.

```{r baseline-join}
collect_metrics(bayes, summarize = FALSE) |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  select(id, tuned = .estimate) |>
  left_join(
    collect_metrics(baseline, summarize = FALSE) |>
      filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
      select(id, fixed = .estimate),
    by = "id"
  )
```

Each row compares the two runs on one fold. A difference between their
two nested estimates is not a test, as `vignette("estimate")` explains.

## A set of workflows

`nested_workflow_map()` runs every workflow of a `workflow_set()` through
one nested function on one design. Our set holds the random forest, a
linear model with nothing to tune, and a linear model on a tuned number of
principal components. The components workflow takes its own grid through
`option_add()`, which overrides the call's `grid` for that workflow alone.

```{r wset}
pca <- recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) |>
  step_normalize(all_predictors()) |>
  step_pca(all_predictors(), num_comp = tune())

wset <- as_workflow_set(
  forest = wf,
  linear = workflow(mpg ~ ., linear_reg()),
  components = workflow(pca, linear_reg())
) |>
  option_add(grid = tibble(num_comp = 1:4), id = "components")

set.seed(7)
mapped <- nested_workflow_map(
  wset,
  fn = "nested_tune_grid",
  resamples = folds,
  grid = grid
)

mapped
```

The linear model has nothing to tune, so it ran through
`nested_fit_resamples()`, and the print marks it "no tuning". The collect
functions stack their tables under each workflow's id.

```{r wset-metrics}
collect_metrics(mapped)
```

`autoplot()` puts the workflows side by side, one point per outer fold.

```{r wset-performance, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Two panels, one per metric, with the three workflows along the x axis, one point per outer fold and a dashed rule at each workflow's nested estimate."}
autoplot(mapped, type = "performance")
```

Picking the best workflow by these estimates is a selection that no outer
loop scored. For a workflow chosen in advance, `nested_final_fit(mapped,
id = "forest")` fits the model to deploy, and its rows in
`collect_metrics(mapped)` are the numbers to report.
